summary:
Field Shift is an interactive crop-planning dashboard that helps farmers explore how climate conditions relate to wheat rotation decisions. Using 35 years of NASA POWER historical data for a Central Kansas reference location, it visualizes temperature, precipitation, and root-zone wetness, allowing users to compare individual years and growing seasons against a historical baseline.

The application connects these climate signals to research questions around three rotation pathways: wheat with cover crops, legumes, or forage sorghum. A separate Future Predictions tab provides clearly labeled, interactive mock scenarios for exploring possible changes in temperature and rainfall.

Field Shift addresses the challenge of making complex climate data accessible and useful for agricultural planning. By bringing historical evidence, understandable visualizations, and rotation considerations into one interface, it supports more informed conversations about water availability, soil management, and climate adaptation. It complements local expertise rather than claiming to predict yields or prescribe the best rotation.
details:
Field Shift is a browser-based prototype that makes historical climate information easier to explore when investigating wheat rotation strategies. It uses NASA POWER monthly data from 1991–2025 for a Central Kansas reference point at 38.50° N, 98.00° W.

Our Python backend processes downloaded climate records, handles missing observations, and calculates annual and October–June growing-season summaries. The dashboard displays temperature, accumulated precipitation, and modeled root-zone wetness, with comparisons against a 1991–2020 baseline. Users can change the year and period, explore charts, and download historical data.

Rotation Studio presents three research candidates: wheat with cover crops, legumes/pulses, or forage sorghum. It identifies considerations and evidence needed for local evaluation without claiming a validated ranking or yield forecast. A separate Future Predictions tab lets users adjust warming, rainfall, and planning-horizon assumptions. These calculations are explicitly labeled as illustrative mock scenarios, not NASA climate projections.

The application uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG charts, a Python data-processing pipeline, and Vercel hosting. OpenAI Codex assisted with frontend implementation, debugging, testing, deployment configuration, mock scenario logic, and project text.

Our intended impact is to make climate evidence accessible for agricultural planning conversations. The prototype currently covers one reference location. Field-specific soil inputs, farmer priorities, crop-response models, and independently validated recommendations remain future work.
